title: The case for mixed-ability classes
subject: reading

paragraphs.text: Picture this scene. It’s an English literature lesson in a UK school, and the teacher has just read an extract from Shakespeare’s Romeo and Juliet with a class of 15-year-olds. He’s given some of the students copies of No Fear Shakespeare, a kid-friendly translation of the original. For three students, even these literacy demands are beyond them. Another girl simply can’t focus and he gives her pens and paper to draw with. The teacher can ask the No Fear group to identify the key characters and maybe provide a tentative plot summary. He can ask most of the class about character development, and five of them might be able to support their statements with textual evidence. Now two curious students are wondering whether Shakespeare dvocates living a life of moderation or one of passionate engagement.

As a teacher myself, I’d think my lesson would be going rather well if the discussion went as described above. But wouldn’t this kind of class work better if there weren’t a such a huge gap between the top and the bottom? If we put all the kids who needed literacy support into one class, and all the students who want to discuss the virtue of moderation into another?

The practice of ‘streaming’, or ‘tracking’, involves separating students into classes depending on their diagnosed levels of attainment. At a macro level, it requires the establishment of academically selective schools for the brightest students, and comprehensive schools for the rest. Within schools, it means selecting students into a ‘stream’ of general ability, or ‘sets’ of subject specific ability. The practice is intuitively appealing to almost every stakeholder.

I have heard the mixed-ability model attacked by way of analogy: a group hike. The fittest in the group take the lead and set a brisk pace, only to have to stop and wait every 20 minutes. This is frustrating, and their enthusiasm wanes. Meanwhile, the slowest ones are not only embarrassed but physically struggling to keep up. What’s worse, they never get a long enough break. They honestly just want to quit. Hiking, they feel, is not for them.

Mixed-ability classes bore students, frustrate parents and burn out teachers. The brightest ones will never summit Mount Qomolangma, and the stragglers won’t enjoy the lovely stroll in the park they are perhaps more suited to. Individuals suffer at the demands of the collective, mediocrity prevails. So: is learning like hiking?

The current pedagogical paradigm is arguably that of constructivism, which emerged out of the work of psychologist Lev Vygotsky. In the 1930s, Vygotsky emphasised the importance of targeting a student’s specific ‘zone of proximal development’ (ZPD). This is the gap between what they can achieve only with support – teachers, textbooks, worked examples, parents and so on – and what they can achieve independently. The purpose of teaching is to provide and then gradually remove this ‘scaffolding’ until they are autonomous. If we accept this model, it follows that streaming students with similar ZPDs would be an efficient and effective solution. And that forcing everyone on the same hike – regardless of aptitude – would be madness.

Despite all this, there is limited empirical evidence to suggest that streaming results in better outcomes for students. Professor John Hattie, director of the Melbourne Education Research Institute, notes that ‘tracking has minimal effects on learning outcomes’. What is more, streaming appears to significantly – and negatively – affect those students assigned to the lowest sets. These students tend to have much higher representation of low

socioeconomic class. Less significant is the small benefit for those lucky clever students in the higher sets. The overall result is that the smart stay smart and the dumb get dumber, further entrenching the social divide.

In the latest update of Hattie’s influential meta-analysis of factors influencing student achievement, one of the most significant factors is the teachers’ estimate of achievement. Streaming students by diagnosed achievement automatically limits what the teacher feels the student is capable of. Meanwhile, in a mixed environment, teachers’ estimates need to be more diverse and flexible.

While streaming might seem to help teachers effectively target a student’s ZPD, it can underestimate the importance of peer-to-peer learning. A crucial aspect of constructivist theory is the role of the MKO – ‘moreknowledgeable other’ – in knowledge construction. While teachers are traditionally the MKOs in classrooms, the value of knowledgeable student peers must not go unrecognised either.

I find it amazing to watch students get over an idea to their peers in ways that I would never think of. They operate with different language tools and different social tools from teachers and, having just learnt it themselves, they possess similar cognitive structures to their struggling classmates. There is also something exciting about passing on skills and knowledge that you yourself have just mastered – a certain pride and zeal, a certain freshness to the interaction between ‘teacher’ and ‘learner’ that is often lost by the expert for whom the steps are obvious and the joy of discovery forgotten.

Having a variety of different abilities in a collaborative learning environment provides valuable resources for helping students meet their learning needs, not to mention improving their communication and social skills. And today, more than ever, we need the many to flourish – not suffer at the expense of a few bright stars. Once a year, I go on a hike with my class, a mixed bunch of students. It is challenging. The fittest students realise they need to encourage the reluctant. There are lookouts who report back, and extra items to carry for others. We make it – together.

groups.instruction:
Questions 27–30

Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.

questions.prompt: The writer describes the Romeo and Juliet lesson in order to demonstrate

options.text: how few students are interested in literature.
how a teacher handles a range of learning needs.
how unsuitable Shakespeare is for most teenagers.
how weaker students can disrupt their classmates’ learning.

questions.explanation:
虽然这部一模一样出现在原文中的莎士比亚名著本身非常容易定位，但考生很快便会发现：仅仅只是看懂包含它的一句话，远不足以解答题目。与其一次次怀揣美好希望又一次次被现实所打击，不如从一开始就直接默认“做一道单选题可能就需要看一段内容”这个现实，反而可能会在遇到有些题并不考查一整段而是可以仅靠两三句话就能做得出来时，有意外惊喜之感。综合全段内容，可以看出在这个课堂里，既有大多数“学民”水平有限无法直接读莎士比亚原著，而是需要看改写后的简单版本，也有少量“学渣”完全无法集中精力在课堂上，只能拿纸笔画画玩儿，还有些许“学霸”已经开始思考戏剧背后的抽象人生意义，而老师则需要在同一个课堂里同时应对这些不同状态的学生。用这个全盘认知来对比四个选项，可得最合适的答案应为B项：how a teacher handles a range of learning needs.（一位教师如何处理一系列的不同学习需求。）

A项：how few students are interested in literature.（多么少的学生对文学感兴趣。）本项与原文唯一沾边的地方，恐怕就是“学生”和“文学”这两个词在第一段里出现过了。孩子们是否对学习的这门课程感兴趣？原文完全没有提及过任何这个方面的信息。

C项：how unsuitable Shakespeare is for most teenagers.（莎士比亚戏剧对于大多数青少年来说是多么不合适的读物。）这一项的干扰性可能略强一些，因为第一段里确实说到了教师为一些学生提供了简写版的莎翁剧本，而另外三个学生则连这种简写版都会觉得难。但是，这是否足以证明“大多数年轻人”都不适合？显然文章里这几个学生的数量还远不足以构成充分必要条件，是一个逻辑谬误。

D项：how weaker students can disrupt their classmates’ learning.（能力较弱的学生会如何干扰其同班同学的学习。）第一段里确实有提及有些学生水平较弱，但却并没有说到他们是否影响、打扰到了其他学生的正常学习秩序。如果这是一道判断题的话，本选项就是一个妥妥的NOT GIVEN选项。

questions.prompt: What does the writer say about streaming in the third paragraph?

options.text: It has a very broad appeal.
It favours cleverer students.
It is relatively simple to implement.
It works better in some schools than others.

questions.explanation:
这种问“作者在某一段里对什么对象提出了什么看法”的问题，优点和缺点都非常明显。优点是完全不用耗费任何时间去定位，缺点则是基本无法指望靠只看段落中的某一句两句话而得出正确结论。具体到本题上来说，第三段的篇幅其实并不长，一共由四句话组成。但考生就是需要看完全段才能笃定得出结论，因为最直接提示了正确选项的内容，来自本段的最后一句话，甚至原文句中的appealing这个词，考生即使不认识词义，单凭单词的“长相”，都能对应到正确答案中的appeal。问题是，要做这个动作，先得看到本段的最后一句，所以还是要看完全段内容，不要心存侥幸，方能更有把握地锁定答案为A项：It has a very broad appeal.（它有着广泛的吸引力。）

B项：It favours cleverer students.（它更青睐比较聪明的学生。）本段内容只是客观陈述和解释了分班制的定义和执行时需要满足哪些条件，并没有给出任何点评性信息，是一个“无中生有”式的弱干扰选项。

C项：It is relatively simple to implement.（它相对比较容易执行。）本段的第二和第三句话里，分别说到了要执行这种分班制，宏观层面上和在某一所学校内部，各自需要满足什么条件。如果一定要从这两句话中进行推导引申，那么恐怕这种制度反而属于不那么容易执行的类型。当然，考生实际并不需要做这样的延伸性发挥，只需确认这项并不是第三段里对分班制的核心描述、不是正确答案即可。

D项：It works better in some schools than others.（它在一些学校中比在其他学校里起效更好。）这个选项与B项类似，也是文章中完全没有提到过的信息。

questions.prompt: What idea is suggested by the reference to Mount Qomolangma in the fifth paragraph?

options.text: students following unsuitable paths
students attempting interesting tasks
students not achieving their full potential
students not being aware of their limitations

questions.explanation:
本题的难度不高。首先是因为题干中不但直接告知了要去第五段找，而且还进一步给出了“珠穆朗玛峰”这个大写定位线索；其次，虽然只看包含这个大写信息的一句不见得能帮助考生马上锁定答案，但本段篇幅很短，一共只有四句话，采用平行阅读策略的考生只需要一路顺位阅读下来，应当不难看出这里的暗喻用法。如果对这个定位句本身的句法结构和句意有疑惑，可以参见前文“佳句赏析”中的第一句。耐心读懂第五段大意，特别是看懂了用“登顶最高峰”来暗喻“达到学术上的最高水平”，即可确认答案应为C项：students not achieving their full potential（学生们没能实现自己潜力的最大值）

本题中的另外三个选项，基本都属于“完全未在段中被提到”的类型，干扰性不大。

A项：students following unsuitable paths（学生们走上了不适合的路径）

B项：students attempting interesting tasks（学生们尝试有趣的任务）

D项：students not being aware of their limitations（学生们没有意识到自身局限）

questions.prompt: What does the word 'scaffolding' in the sixth paragraph refer to?

options.text: the factors which prevent a student from learning effectively
the environment where most of a student’s learning takes place
the assistance given to a student in their initial stages of learning
the setting of appropriate learning targets for a student’s aptitude

questions.explanation:
本题其实证明了这样一点：考生自身的知识结构和储备对于顺利解题绝对有着许多潜在的好处。了解或学习过TKT或CELTA资质证书的考生，恐怕在直接看到scaffolding这个术语的时候，就可以凭借对其了解而直接解题，甚至都不需要借助本文文意。当然，若是没有接触过这套国际教资体系内的知识，凭借文章描述内容也完全可以答题。

与上一题类似，虽然考生可以直接靠带引号的“脚手架”一词定位到本段倒数第三句，但还是在有了前文阅读的知识背景下才能更好地理解本句意思，明白所谓的“脚手架”指的是在一开始给学生一些帮助，让他们能顺利度过初始阶段而逐渐变得更加独立自主。由此可以最终锁定正确答案应为C项：the assistance given to a student in their initial stages of learning（在一个学生的起始学习阶段提供给他们的帮助）

A项：the factors which prevent a student from learning effectively（阻碍一个学生有效学习的因素）本项与第六段唯一的关联，可能是题干中的副词effectively与原文倒数第二句中的形容词effective出自同一个词群（word family）。除此之外，题干整句所表达的意思在原文中完全未被提及过。

B项：the environment where most of a student’s learning takes place（一个学生在其中进行自己大部分学习行为的环境）本项与上面的A项类似，也是一个无中生有的内容。

D项：the setting of appropriate learning targets for a student’s aptitude（根据一个学生的资质为其设定合适的学习目标）本段中确实谈及了学生各有不同资质这个话题，但这与倒数第三句中使用“脚手架”时所说的内容并没有直接关联。考生只需理解到这个程度，应该就不会被此项所混淆干扰。

Questions 31–35

35. 本题的位置距离前四道题略远，但对于采用了平行阅读的考生来说，要顺序阅读到此处，根据句意看出教师由于学生已经根据水平和表现被分了班、因而对他们能力的看法受到了局限，应该就能顺利锁定词库中的对应项：B lower expectations。

groups.contextHtml:
Is streaming effective?


According to Professor John Hattie of the Melbourne Education Research Institute, there is very little indication that streaming leads to [31] ______  . He points out that, in schools which use streaming, the most significant impact is on those students placed in the [32] ______  , especially where a large proportion of them have [33] ______  . Meanwhile, for the [34] ______  , there appears to be only minimal advantage. A further issue is that teachers tend to have [35] ______  of students in streamed groups.

groups.instruction:
Questions 36–40

Do the following statements agree with the views of the writer in Reading Passage 3?

Choose

YES if the statement agrees with the views of the writer

NO if the statement contradicts the views of the writer

NOT GIVEN if it is impossible to say what the writer thinks about this

questions.prompt: The Vygotsky model of education supports the concept of a mixed-ability class.
questions.explanation: 本题虽然包含着大写人名，可以协助考生直接定位到第六段的第一句，但这句话本身却无法直接帮助判定题干结论，而只是列出了维果斯基的理论：每个学生都有自己当前所处的一个能力区域。耐心阅读接下来的第六段文意，才能逐渐看出：根据这个理论，学生应该被首先确定其所处区域，然后被提供必要帮助直到其可以自主学习进步，因而将处在同一个区域的学生分进同样的班级学习会更高效，反之若是将不同能力学生混杂放进同一个班里将会是疯狂之举。第六段读完，考生才可根据段意的起承转合明白：维果斯基的理论支持的是分班制，这与题干所说的“支持混合能力班级”形成了直白的矛盾抵触，可知正确答案应为NO。

questions.prompt: Some teachers are uncertain about allowing students to take on MKO roles in the classroom.
questions.explanation: 本题的大致出处虽然距离上一题不算很近，但考生可以依靠MKO这个大写信息更快地来到第九段原文。然而，看遍了本段的这几句与MKO有关的句子，也找不到任何地方明确说了“教师是否对学生担当MKO角色有着不确定的态度”，再加上接下来很快在第十段里给出了下一道第38题的答案，因而考生只需遵循“判断题一次对比两道题干”的做法，耐心阅读对比，就能比较笃定本题的答案应为NOT GIVEN。

questions.prompt: It can be rewarding to teach knowledge which you have only recently acquired.
questions.explanation: 本题的难度主要来自于对应原文中两个句子本身的复杂语法结构，其详细分析可以参见前文“佳句赏析”中的第三和第四句。在这里，作者以称得上是热情洋溢的笔触，极力赞美了让那些学得快学得好的孩子来给自己的同学讲解刚学到的知识都会有哪些好处。这当然是传达出了“这种做法非常值得”的意味，与题干内容相符，正确答案应为YES。

questions.prompt: The priority should be to ensure that the highest-achieving students attain their goals.
questions.explanation: 本题的定位与上一道题距离不远，且对应原文句本身和题干都没有包含生僻的认知词汇。虽然没有原样重现的定位词提示，但考生只需耐心顺序阅读、真正看懂句意，应该就不难读懂本段第二句话说的是“我们需要大多数人都能兴旺发展而不是只有一小撮精英光芒四射”，进而明白这与题干说的“优先考虑少数精英达成目标”形成了矛盾抵触，从而得出正确答案应为NO。

questions.prompt: Taking part in collaborative outdoor activities with teachers and classmates can improve student outcomes in the classroom.
questions.explanation: 留给本题进行定位解答的篇幅，一共只剩下最后一段的最后几句话了。读完这几句简短易懂的话以后，考生不难看出：作者在这里只是描述了自己每年都组织全班孩子一起远足爬山，在这其中能力高低不同的学生最终都成功完成了这场集体活动。至于接下来孩子们在课堂里的表现如何，是否学习成绩有所提升，本文并没有任何跟进说明，因此正确答案应为NOT GIVEN。

articleHtml:
The case for mixed-ability classes


Picture this scene. It’s an English literature lesson in a UK school, and the teacher has just read an extract from Shakespeare’s Romeo and Juliet with a class of 15-year-olds. He’s given some of the students copies of No Fear Shakespeare, a kid-friendly translation of the original. For three students, even these literacy demands are beyond them. Another girl simply can’t focus and he gives her pens and paper to draw with. The teacher can ask the No Fear group to identify the key characters and maybe provide a tentative plot summary. He can ask most of the class about character development, and five of them might be able to support their statements with textual evidence. Now two curious students are wondering whether Shakespeare dvocates living a life of moderation or one of passionate engagement.

As a teacher myself, I’d think my lesson would be going rather well if the discussion went as described above. But wouldn’t this kind of class work better if there weren’t a such a huge gap between the top and the bottom? If we put all the kids who needed literacy support into one class, and all the students who want to discuss the virtue of moderation into another?

The practice of ‘streaming’, or ‘tracking’, involves separating students into classes depending on their diagnosed levels of attainment. At a macro level, it requires the establishment of academically selective schools for the brightest students, and comprehensive schools for the rest. Within schools, it means selecting students into a ‘stream’ of general ability, or ‘sets’ of subject specific ability. The practice is intuitively appealing to almost every stakeholder.

I have heard the mixed-ability model attacked by way of analogy: a group hike. The fittest in the group take the lead and set a brisk pace, only to have to stop and wait every 20 minutes. This is frustrating, and their enthusiasm wanes. Meanwhile, the slowest ones are not only embarrassed but physically struggling to keep up. What’s worse, they never get a long enough break. They honestly just want to quit. Hiking, they feel, is not for them. 

Mixed-ability classes bore students, frustrate parents and burn out teachers. The brightest ones will never summit Mount Qomolangma, and the stragglers won’t enjoy the lovely stroll in the park they are perhaps more suited to. Individuals suffer at the demands of the collective, mediocrity prevails. So: is learning like hiking?

The current pedagogical paradigm is arguably that of constructivism, which emerged out of the work of psychologist Lev Vygotsky. In the 1930s, Vygotsky emphasised the importance of targeting a student’s specific ‘zone of proximal development’ (ZPD). This is the gap between what they can achieve only with support – teachers, textbooks, worked examples, parents and so on – and what they can achieve independently. The purpose of teaching is to provide and then gradually remove this ‘scaffolding’ until they are autonomous. If we accept this model, it follows that streaming students with similar ZPDs would be an efficient and effective solution. And that forcing everyone on the same hike – regardless of aptitude – would be madness.

Despite all this, there is limited empirical evidence to suggest that streaming results in better outcomes for students. Professor John Hattie, director of the Melbourne Education Research Institute, notes that ‘tracking has minimal effects on learning outcomes’. What is more, streaming appears to significantly – and negatively – affect those students assigned to the lowest sets. These students tend to have much higher representation of low
socioeconomic class. Less significant is the small benefit for those lucky clever students in the higher sets. The overall result is that the smart stay smart and the dumb get dumber, further entrenching the social divide.

In the latest update of Hattie’s influential meta-analysis of factors influencing student achievement, one of the most significant factors is the teachers’ estimate of achievement. Streaming students by diagnosed achievement automatically limits what the teacher feels the student is capable of. Meanwhile, in a mixed environment, teachers’ estimates need to be more diverse and flexible.

While streaming might seem to help teachers effectively target a student’s ZPD, it can underestimate the importance of peer-to-peer learning. A crucial aspect of constructivist theory is the role of the MKO – ‘moreknowledgeable other’ – in knowledge construction. While teachers are traditionally the MKOs in classrooms, the value of knowledgeable student peers must not go unrecognised either.

I find it amazing to watch students get over an idea to their peers in ways that I would never think of. They operate with different language tools and different social tools from teachers and, having just learnt it themselves, they possess similar cognitive structures to their struggling classmates. There is also something exciting about passing on skills and knowledge that you yourself have just mastered – a certain pride and zeal, a certain freshness to the interaction between ‘teacher’ and ‘learner’ that is often lost by the expert for whom the steps are obvious and the joy of discovery forgotten. 

Having a variety of different abilities in a collaborative learning environment provides valuable resources for helping students meet their learning needs, not to mention improving their communication and social skills. And today, more than ever, we need the many to flourish – not suffer at the expense of a few bright stars. Once a year, I go on a hike with my class, a mixed bunch of students. It is challenging. The fittest students realise they need to encourage the reluctant. There are lookouts who report back, and extra items to carry for others. We make it – together.
